newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets gyrate but polls not set in stone.
newsitem.headline: French markets gyrate but polls not set in stone.

text.p: Polls are making financial markets shudder in France ahead of a May 25-June 1 parliamentary election but pollsters and analysts warned on Friday that voter opinion as well as early poll results are far from set in stone.

Markets gyrated on Thursday when an IPSOS poll for the weekly Le Point showed France's governing centre-right ahead by only a wafer-thin margin in the two-round election, with the opposition Socialists within reach of a parliamentary majority.

But pollsters freely acknowledged their polls were nothing more than "a snapshot of the moment" and there was significant uncertainty at this stage of the campaign, both in their polls and in voters' minds.
Trading in the markets on the basis of a single poll "shows that people do not learn from their mistakes," joked Jerome Sainte-Marie of Louis Harris France.
In the IPSOS poll, for example, 31 percent did not say how they intended to vote, indicating sizeable indecision at the early stages of a short campaign period.

IPSOS projected 292 seats for the centre-right, 256 seats for the Socialists, 28 seats for the Communists and one for the far-right National Front based on a complex statistical model that even IPSOS concedes leaves many questions unanswered.
"Statistically speaking, they (the majority and the Left) are level," said Pierre Giacometti of IPSOS. "But what was true yesterday is no longer true today."
He said the IPSOS projection concluded that 148 seats would be won by five to 10 percentage points and another 182 by fewer than five points if the election were held today.
A shift in voter preference of just one percentage point could alter the final result in 30 districts, Giacometti said.

In addition, a low turnout in the June 1 run-off round, in which numerous three-way races are expected between majority, leftist and National Front candidates, "could drastically alter the results," he said.
IPSOS and other French pollsters defend the statistical models used to project results as accurate at any given moment.
But they also, to varying degrees, acknowledge the models' shortcomings in accurately predicting final results.
"I have no confidence in this model," said Giacometti. Every time I stick my nose into it, I find myself very disturbed. There are so many factors that enter into the calculation."
He said it was possible pollsters would not be in a position to accurately project this year's election outcome until the night before the second round vote.

Though deputies are elected from one of 577 individual districts, pollsters statistical models typically give short shrift to local issues because they rely heavily on voters' stated preference for national political parties, filtered by past voting patterns.
Nation-wide polls in France typically rely on the views of about a thousand individuals aged 18 and over -- on average, fewer than two per constituency.
Nonetheless, "these models are usually used with great success. They work," said Stephane Rozes of the CSA polling firm.
"The problem is voter preference (rather than small sample size). A change of one or two percent can affect dozens of seats," he said.
"You can always improve your methods, but the system works well enough. If not, our clients would not be spending so much money on our polls," Rozes said.
